addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

- omarchy: REQUIRED for end-user customization of Linux desktop, window manager, or system config. Use when editing ~/.config/hypr/, ~/.config/waybar/, ~/.config/walker/, ~/.config/alacritty/, ~/.config/foot/, ~/.config/kitty/, ~/.config/ghostty/, ~/.config/mako/, or ~/.config/omarchy/. Triggers: Hyprland, window rules, animations, keybindings, monitors, gaps, borders, blur, opacity, waybar, walker, terminal config, themes, wallpaper, night light, idle, lock screen, screenshots, reminders, layer rules, workspace settings, display config, and user-facing omarchy commands. Excludes Omarchy source development in ~/.local/share/omarchy/ and `omarchy dev` workflows.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

# Long Term Vision + Goal

This project explores the most efficient ways to run a variety of AI/LLM generations on **Vulkan** using the AMD AI MAX+ 395 "Strix Halo" platform, with gfx1151 and RDNA3.5. 

Ultimately we want to be able to run these tasks:
  1. Speech to Text via Nvidia's `parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3`:
    * https://huggingface.co/nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3
    * https://arxiv.org/html/2509.14128v2
  2. Text generation via Qwen's `Qwen3.8-Next-Flash`:
    * https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
    * https://arxiv.org/html/2608.30320v1
    * We'll need to quantise the weights once we've determined the most efficient method for the hardware
  3. Text to Speech via Hexgrad's `kokoro-82M`:
    * https://huggingface.co/hexgrad/Kokoro-82M
    * https://arxiv.org/html/2306.07691v2
  4. Image generation via Tongyi's `z-image-turbo`:
    * https://huggingface.co/Tongyi-MAI/Z-Image-Turbo
    * https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22699v5
    * With this smaller model to generate in-progress previews: 
      * https://huggingface.co/madebyollin/taef1
  5. Compute embeddings via Qwen's `Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B`:
    * https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B
    * https://arxiv.org/html/2506.05176v3

We will ultimately serve up a HTTP API serving these features, in Go.

1	# LLM2 — the review, the hypotheses checked, and the next priority list
2	
3	> **Written 2026-09-17**, as a review of `LLM.md` at L8c-7 / L9a. `LLM.md`
4	> stays the stage log; this file is the forward-looking list. Same
5	> conventions: history to `TODO.md`, closed findings to `research/`.
6	
7	## Where this stands, in five lines
8	
9	- **Decode 32.93 tok/s** against llama.cpp's 25.15 — **1.31x** — at a
10	  measured bank of 4.281 GB a token, a ceiling of 56.5 at the bus and 53.0
11	  at the rate dispatches reach. P1 attributed the step to the dispatch and
12	  took the n-gram gather's sixteen serialised page faults out of it; P1a
13	  fused the hyper-connection boundary, 1501 dispatches a pass to 1407; P1c
14	  put the step in one pre-recorded command buffer, −1.90 ms a token
15	  (measured 25.4 → 26.7 on a day the machine itself was 29% slower — see
16	  P1c's environment finding before comparing across days).
17	- **Prefill 1089.2 tok/s** at ubatch 2048 against 391.4 — **2.78x** — and
18	  668.1 at 512. The original L2a target of ~1150 is 95% reached. P1a's fusion
19	  is +1.7% of it at 2048 and nothing at 512, because the residual crosses the
20	  MALL in between.
21	- **Perplexity 4.1787 against our 4.0289 — +3.72%** (and +3.59% against the
22	  reference's own 4.0340), with five of six dense families at 4.5 bits and
23	  additivity holding to 0.01 pp.
24	- **Served**: `cmd/serve -llm`, three envelopes over one loop, prefix reuse.
25	- ~~**One correctness cliff**~~: **closed at P0 (2026-09-18)**. It was
26	  amdgpu's gfx ring watchdog killing any submit that holds the ring past
27	  **2 s** — not rows, layers, bytes or residency. The recorder chunks by time
28	  now, and prefill runs to **8192 rows at 1213.5 tok/s, 3.10x**, still
29	  climbing where llama.cpp's plateaus.
30	
31	Phase 1 is done, phase 2's kernel half is done, and phase 2's width half is
32	one trivial family (`ple_proj`) from done. The plan as originally drawn —
33	run it, profile it, then optimise — executed, and the reference is beaten on
34	both axes. **The competition from here is our own ceiling, not llama.cpp.**
35	
36	---
37	
38	## The hypotheses, checked
39	
40	| hypothesis | verdict |
41	|---|---|
42	| **"Decode is DRAM-bound by weight bytes"** (the premise of D3, L8a-L8c) | **Was true, is now 79% true, and P1 says where the rest is.** Through L8b, measured ≈ ceiling: 14.71 tok/s against 15.4 GB-derived numbers. Today the weight-streaming dispatches are **24.05 ms of a 30.52 ms step, 79%** — but they run at **178 GB/s against the 227 a dispatch reaches**, so 5.54 ms of that is shape rather than bytes, and another 3.46 ms of dispatches stream no weight at all. The binding constraint has moved from *how many bytes* to *how the dispatches are shaped*: `hyper_conn` at 114.6 GB/s and `moe.down` at 147.5 against `moe.up`'s 200.6 off the same bank. |
43	| **"The cost of 4 bits runs inverse to the bytes"** (L8c-1's headline) | **Retired by its own successors.** The pp-per-GB ranking over 145 chunks is bimodal: `deltanet` 0.87, `hyper_conn` 0.93, `lm_head` 2.59, `full_attn` 5.52 — and the split is presence (36 layers / 97 mixers vs 12 layers / 1 matrix), not size. |
44	| **"An 8-chunk screen predicts a family's corpus cost"** | **Retired, four ways.** +0.40→+0.82, −0.30→+0.93, +0.90→+0.31, +1.05→+1.65. A screen does not bound, does not fix the sign, does not rank. Every future width call needs a 145-chunk run (8 min — affordable). |
45	| **"Corpus deltas add"** (the asymmetric form's additivity) | **Confirmed to 0.01 pp across four families** — where the symmetric form compounded 11.7% into 18.5%. This is now a *tool*: plans are composable from measured per-family deltas (see idea 4). Caveat: only demonstrated on the asymmetric form at 4.5 bits. |
46	| **D14: "a bank that fits the MALL pays only its unpack"** | **Confirmed with its boundary, four blocks, both signs, one rule.** Closed as a hypothesis; it is now a design fact. |
47	| **D12's 4 KB formulation** | **Weakened at L8c-6** (no rung is a whole multiple and the spread is still 1.65x); the operative half — *re-measure when the width changes* — stands and is what caught it. |
48	| **"Residency is free"** (L6a-4) | **Confirmed at ≤2560 rows — and the >2560 stall is plausibly its boundary.** The untested suspicion in the open question is exactly residency (~80 GB pinned + 28.8 GB mmap + arenas that grow with rows). If P0 confirms it, L6a-4 gains a cliff. |
49	| **"Context is cheap here"** (the QSA table in `LLM.md`) | **Priced, never demonstrated.** The arithmetic says 6.8 GB of KV at 262k and a capped 2051-cell read per step; the graph has never completed past 2560 rows. Currently an *inference*, not a measurement — P0 gates it. |
50	| **D16: a rung above 242 GB/s is not a DRAM measurement** | **Confirmed and generalising**: every one-token ladder screened so far was choosing rungs against an L3 hit. Standing rule: re-screen a ladder before acting on it. |
51	
52	---
53	
54	## The decode budget, re-derived honestly
55	
56	The 56.5 tok/s ceiling counts streamed weights only. A token also moves:
57	
58	    DeltaNet state, 36 x 3.1 MB, read + write     ~0.22 GB
59	    KV + indexer at 2k context                    ~0.05 GB
60	    activations, rings, logits row                ~0.01 GB
61	                                                  --------
62	    honest per-token traffic                      ~4.56 GB  -> ~53 tok/s
63	
64	Measured 31.5 tok/s is 31.7 ms a token; 4.56 GB at the best measured
65	dispatch rate (227 GB/s) is ~20 ms. **~12 ms a token — 37% of the step — is
66	not accounted for by streaming bytes at any achievable rate**, and no
67	attribution has been run since L8e.
68	
69	**P1 ran it, and the estimate was right to 0.01 ms.** The step is 30.52 ms
70	after the gather fix, and it sums:
71	
72	    weight-streaming dispatches, 4.281 GB at 178 GB/s      24.05 ms
73	      of which, over the 18.86 ms the same bytes take at 227   5.54
74	    dispatches that stream no weight (scan, moves, norms,
75	      permutations, combines)                               3.46 ms
76	    host: record 1.127, gather 0.902, hand-over 0.828,
77	      sample 0.142, detokenize + emit 0.007                 3.01 ms
78	    unattributed                                            0.005 ms
79	
80	**5.54 + 3.46 + 3.01 = 12.01.** The candidates list above was almost exactly
81	wrong in its ordering: the sampler and detokenizer are **0.15 ms together**,
82	host record and submit are 1.96, and the two real items are dispatches off
83	the bus (`hyper_conn` at 114.6 GB/s, `moe.down` at 147.5) and the 3.46 ms of
84	dispatches nobody had counted because they read no weights at all. The one
85	candidate that was under-rated is the PLE host gather, which was 2.24 ms and
86	is now 0.90 — see P1's finding 1.
87	
88	---
89	
90	## Ideas that are not in the current plan
91	
92	1. ~~**Re-attribute the decode step**~~ **— done (P1), and it was the single
93	   highest information-per-hour item on the list**: it paid for itself with
94	   the gather fix before the analysis was written, and it demoted idea 2
95	   from first to fourth.
96	2. **A pre-recorded, reusable decode command buffer.** IDEAS §4.2 was never
97	   carried into this vertical. The decode graph is shape-stable token to
98	   token — **1501 dispatches** (P1 counted them; the ~490 here was the
99	   pre-L7d submit count), same buffers; only the position and the token id
100	   change. Record once, feed the varying scalars through a small uniform
101	   buffer (or indirect dispatch) instead of re-recording. **P1 priced it:
102	   1.127 ms of recording plus 0.828 of hand-over, 6.4% of the step, about
103	   +2.2 tok/s** — real, and, with P1a done and P1b measured empty, now the
104	   front of the list.
105	3. **MTP needs a rollback story before it needs a kernel.** Speculation on a
106	   *recurrent* model is not the usual KV-truncate: a rejected draft must
107	   rewind (a) 36 DeltaNet states — checkpoint/restore of 113 MB, ~0.3 ms as
108	   a device copy, fine but must be designed in; (b) both convolution rings,
109	   whose stores are currently pure writes addressed by position; (c) the KV
110	   cache and pooled indexer blocks (easy — truncate); (d) the host-side id
111	   list the trigram hash reads. And verification runs at M = 2-8, where D15
112	   *refuses* the GEMV path by design — the M=2..8 GEMM/GEMV crossover
113	   (IDEAS §1.5) has never been measured on this model's shapes. A half-page
114	   design doc first; it changes the state-object API (P5).
115	4. **The accuracy knapsack.** Additivity + per-family corpus deltas mean the
116	   shipped plan is now a solvable trade, and the uniform plan is provably
117	   not optimal in pp-per-GB: `full_attn` buys 0.299 GB a token for +1.65%
118	   while `deltanet` buys 1.07 GB for +0.93%. Two composable options, both
119	   computable *today* from numbers already in `results/`:
120	   - `full_attn` back to int8: ~4.58 GB a token, ~52.8 ceiling, **~+2.07%**.
121	   - `full_attn` at 5.5 bits: `sim.go` can grade a q5_k arm in one 8-min
122	     run **before any kernel exists** — likely most of the bytes back for a
123	     fraction of the 1.65.
124	   Nothing forces uniform 4.5. Decide with numbers, record it as D18.
125	5. **A second corpus, and one downstream eval.** +3.72% rests entirely on
126	   wikitext-2. The instrument is corpus-agnostic — one run on code or on
127	   chat-formatted text is 8 minutes — and the HTTP API makes a small
128	   task-level screen (a few hundred multiple-choice items) an evening. Cheap
129	   insurance before the widths are declared shipped.
130	6. **The DeltaNet state's width.** 0.22 GB a token of the honest budget is
131	   f32 state traffic. fp16 state halves it (+~1.3 tok/s of ceiling) — but
132	   the recurrence accumulates, which is exactly where fp16 goes wrong.
133	   Gradeable end-to-end with the ppl instrument; low priority, but it is
134	   the only remaining per-token traffic nobody has named as a lever.
135	7. **Long-context gates, the day P0 lands**: perplexity at ctx 8k with the
136	   selection biting hard, decode tok/s flatness against context (QSA's
137	   whole promise), and a needle test through the API. None exist because
138	   none *can* yet.
139	8. **Batching × recurrence.** "Batching amortises the dense 76%" is carried
140	   from the phase-3 sketch, but each concurrent sequence owns 113 MB of
141	   DeltaNet state, its own rings and its own KV — the served graph is one
142	   sequence's today. The open product question ("will the API ever serve
143	   more than one stream?") should be answered before P5/P6 ordering is
144	   final, because if yes, batching may beat MTP for the same effort.
145	9. ~~**Reconcile the 0.38 GB**~~ **— closed at P1.** It is the MoE router
146	   (0.252 GB) and the shared expert (0.251), which the checkpoint inventory
147	   files under "dense, every token" and L8b's table files with the MoE, less
148	   L8b-1's doubled `inject` rows, `PLEGPU`'s halves and rounding. Both
149	   counts were right; they partitioned the same tensors differently. Every
150	   ceiling is now quoted on **4.281 GB a token**.
151	
152	---
153	
154	## The priority list
155	
156	### ~~P0 — the >2560-row stall~~  *(**done**, 2026-09-18)*
157	
158	**It was amdgpu's gfx ring watchdog, and none of the four hypotheses above.**
159	A submit that holds the gfx ring past **2.0 s** is killed and the ring reset;

# LLM2 — the review, the hypotheses checked, and the next priority list

> **Written 2026-09-17**, as a review of `LLM.md` at L8c-7 / L9a. `LLM.md`
> stays the stage log; this file is the forward-looking list. Same
> conventions: history to `TODO.md`, closed findings to `research/`.

## Where this stands, in five lines

- **Decode 32.93 tok/s** against llama.cpp's 25.15 — **1.31x** — at a
  measured bank of 4.281 GB a token, a ceiling of 56.5 at the bus and 53.0
  at the rate dispatches reach. P1 attributed the step to the dispatch and
  took the n-gram gather's sixteen serialised page faults out of it; P1a
  fused the hyper-connection boundary, 1501 dispatches a pass to 1407; P1c
  put the step in one pre-recorded command buffer, −1.90 ms a token
  (measured 25.4 → 26.7 on a day the machine itself was 29% slower — see
  P1c's environment finding before comparing across days).
- **Prefill 1089.2 tok/s** at ubatch 2048 against 391.4 — **2.78x** — and
  668.1 at 512. The original L2a target of ~1150 is 95% reached. P1a's fusion
  is +1.7% of it at 2048 and nothing at 512, because the residual crosses the
  MALL in between.
- **Perplexity 4.1787 against our 4.0289 — +3.72%** (and +3.59% against the
  reference's own 4.0340), with five of six dense families at 4.5 bits and
  additivity holding to 0.01 pp.
- **Served**: `cmd/serve -llm`, three envelopes over one loop, prefix reuse.
- ~~**One correctness cliff**~~: **closed at P0 (2026-09-18)**. It was
  amdgpu's gfx ring watchdog killing any submit that holds the ring past
  **2 s** — not rows, layers, bytes or residency. The recorder chunks by time
  now, and prefill runs to **8192 rows at 1213.5 tok/s, 3.10x**, still
  climbing where llama.cpp's plateaus.

Phase 1 is done, phase 2's kernel half is done, and phase 2's width half is
one trivial family (`ple_proj`) from done. The plan as originally drawn —
run it, profile it, then optimise — executed, and the reference is beaten on
both axes. **The competition from here is our own ceiling, not llama.cpp.**

---

## The hypotheses, checked

| hypothesis | verdict |
|---|---|
| **"Decode is DRAM-bound by weight bytes"** (the premise of D3, L8a-L8c) | **Was true, is now 79% true, and P1 says where the rest is.** Through L8b, measured ≈ ceiling: 14.71 tok/s against 15.4 GB-derived numbers. Today the weight-streaming dispatches are **24.05 ms of a 30.52 ms step, 79%** — but they run at **178 GB/s against the 227 a dispatch reaches**, so 5.54 ms of that is shape rather than bytes, and another 3.46 ms of dispatches stream no weight at all. The binding constraint has moved from *how many bytes* to *how the dispatches are shaped*: `hyper_conn` at 114.6 GB/s and `moe.down` at 147.5 against `moe.up`'s 200.6 off the same bank. |
| **"The cost of 4 bits runs inverse to the bytes"** (L8c-1's headline) | **Retired by its own successors.** The pp-per-GB ranking over 145 chunks is bimodal: `deltanet` 0.87, `hyper_conn` 0.93, `lm_head` 2.59, `full_attn` 5.52 — and the split is presence (36 layers / 97 mixers vs 12 layers / 1 matrix), not size. |
| **"An 8-chunk screen predicts a family's corpus cost"** | **Retired, four ways.** +0.40→+0.82, −0.30→+0.93, +0.90→+0.31, +1.05→+1.65. A screen does not bound, does not fix the sign, does not rank. Every future width call needs a 145-chunk run (8 min — affordable). |
| **"Corpus deltas add"** (the asymmetric form's additivity) | **Confirmed to 0.01 pp across four families** — where the symmetric form compounded 11.7% into 18.5%. This is now a *tool*: plans are composable from measured per-family deltas (see idea 4). Caveat: only demonstrated on the asymmetric form at 4.5 bits. |
| **D14: "a bank that fits the MALL pays only its unpack"** | **Confirmed with its boundary, four blocks, both signs, one rule.** Closed as a hypothesis; it is now a design fact. |
| **D12's 4 KB formulation** | **Weakened at L8c-6** (no rung is a whole multiple and the spread is still 1.65x); the operative half — *re-measure when the width changes* — stands and is what caught it. |
| **"Residency is free"** (L6a-4) | **Confirmed at ≤2560 rows — and the >2560 stall is plausibly its boundary.** The untested suspicion in the open question is exactly residency (~80 GB pinned + 28.8 GB mmap + arenas that grow with rows). If P0 confirms it, L6a-4 gains a cliff. |
| **"Context is cheap here"** (the QSA table in `LLM.md`) | **Priced, never demonstrated.** The arithmetic says 6.8 GB of KV at 262k and a capped 2051-cell read per step; the graph has never completed past 2560 rows. Currently an *inference*, not a measurement — P0 gates it. |
| **D16: a rung above 242 GB/s is not a DRAM measurement** | **Confirmed and generalising**: every one-token ladder screened so far was choosing rungs against an L3 hit. Standing rule: re-screen a ladder before acting on it. |

---

## The decode budget, re-derived honestly

The 56.5 tok/s ceiling counts streamed weights only. A token also moves:

    DeltaNet state, 36 x 3.1 MB, read + write     ~0.22 GB
    KV + indexer at 2k context                    ~0.05 GB
    activations, rings, logits row                ~0.01 GB
                                                  --------
    honest per-token traffic                      ~4.56 GB  -> ~53 tok/s

Measured 31.5 tok/s is 31.7 ms a token; 4.56 GB at the best measured
dispatch rate (227 GB/s) is ~20 ms. **~12 ms a token — 37% of the step — is
not accounted for by streaming bytes at any achievable rate**, and no
attribution has been run since L8e.

**P1 ran it, and the estimate was right to 0.01 ms.** The step is 30.52 ms
after the gather fix, and it sums:

    weight-streaming dispatches, 4.281 GB at 178 GB/s      24.05 ms
      of which, over the 18.86 ms the same bytes take at 227   5.54
    dispatches that stream no weight (scan, moves, norms,
      permutations, combines)                               3.46 ms
    host: record 1.127, gather 0.902, hand-over 0.828,
      sample 0.142, detokenize + emit 0.007                 3.01 ms
    unattributed                                            0.005 ms

**5.54 + 3.46 + 3.01 = 12.01.** The candidates list above was almost exactly
wrong in its ordering: the sampler and detokenizer are **0.15 ms together**,
host record and submit are 1.96, and the two real items are dispatches off
the bus (`hyper_conn` at 114.6 GB/s, `moe.down` at 147.5) and the 3.46 ms of
dispatches nobody had counted because they read no weights at all. The one
candidate that was under-rated is the PLE host gather, which was 2.24 ms and
is now 0.90 — see P1's finding 1.

---

## Ideas that are not in the current plan

1. ~~**Re-attribute the decode step**~~ **— done (P1), and it was the single
   highest information-per-hour item on the list**: it paid for itself with
   the gather fix before the analysis was written, and it demoted idea 2
   from first to fourth.
2. **A pre-recorded, reusable decode command buffer.** IDEAS §4.2 was never
   carried into this vertical. The decode graph is shape-stable token to
   token — **1501 dispatches** (P1 counted them; the ~490 here was the
   pre-L7d submit count), same buffers; only the position and the token id
   change. Record once, feed the varying scalars through a small uniform
   buffer (or indirect dispatch) instead of re-recording. **P1 priced it:
   1.127 ms of recording plus 0.828 of hand-over, 6.4% of the step, about

## Why this order

**P0, P1, P1a and P1b are done, and each of them moved the list.** P1's suspicion —
that the bank had stopped being the binding constraint — is confirmed, and
the replacement is **kernel shape**: four of the five leading items are
dispatches that are too small or the wrong way round, not bytes.

**P1a then sharpened what "too small" means, and it is not what the phrase
suggested.** Fusing the weightless half of the hyper-connection boundary was
worth its estimate (+0.34 tok/s, 94 dispatches, bit-exact); the *bank* half
was not a fusion question at all. A one-token dispatch on this device is
short of **workgroups**, and the down projection's own decode ladder measures
the law on identical bytes: **168 workgroups is 9.26 us where 672 is 5.54**.
`up` sits at 160 workgroups because MODE 1's collapse pins `BN` at 64, and
unpinning it is priced at 0.22 ms a token — real, and not worth every rung's
epilogue on the prefill path.

**P1b looked like the largest item on the list by a factor of four, and it
was the MALL's arithmetic.** The one-token MoE ladder those rungs were chosen
from was an L3 measurement end to end (every GEMV down rung above the bus);
re-run on sixteen cold banks the ranking does not move on any axis, so the
1.9 ms was never there. What is there is a **1.33 ms environment gap** — the
same dispatch is 8-22% slower inside a real step than alone on a cold bank —
which promoted P1c to the front of the list.

**P1c is done and worth its price — 1.90 ms of the estimated 1.96 — and its
lasting lesson is about the instrument, twice over.** Once small: the decode
step's entire varying state was a single uint, so "feed the varying scalars
through a uniform buffer" collapsed to one arena dword and a one-line macro.
Once large: the *machine* moved 8.7 ms a step overnight with yesterday's
binary — every dense-bank kernel 1.6-1.9x slower, every MoE expert rung
unchanged — so P1b's environment gap has a much bigger sibling that lives
across days rather than within a step, and every whole-model number now
needs a same-hour control the way D16 made every ladder need a cold bank.
P2 and P3 still close the accuracy story while additivity and the
instruments are warm, and they are small. P5 is the largest single
multiplier on the list but wants its own design pass, and its multiplier
applies on top of whatever the rest buys, so it loses nothing by going
after.

**The numbers to beat from here, each on its own day's control: 26.7 tok/s
against 25.4 on the slow day this was measured (32.93 against llama.cpp's
25.15 on P1b's day, ~34.9 by arithmetic on that state), 53.0 honest
good-day ceiling at the 227 GB/s dispatches reach — and llama.cpp behind at
every ubatch.**

442	MALL at every width so the narrower bank adds only the unpack's ALU — 6 ms
443	of a 1921 ms pass, and the other three ubatches are faster. And **D12's
444	ladder did not move**: no rung's slab is a whole multiple of 4 KB on this
445	bank, so L7d's rule does not decide it, yet the spread is still 1.65x and
446	the winner is 32 as it was at int8.
447

449	full-attention layers are 0.635 GB of a token, every matrix in the block is a

454	31.41-31.57 — 1.25x llama.cpp — the block 3.5 ms a token to 2.3, a layer
455	57.94 MB to 32.22, residency 80.20 GB to 79.89, and prefill is faster at

457	2048 against 1065.9). The bank is the format twice again — 97 664 projection
458	values and 17 920 output values identical to the same format through `sim.go`
459	on both arrangements of the tail, and chunk for chunk with the simulation over
460	eight chunks — plus a third check this family needed and the others did not,
461	because the decode GEMV has to derive the fused projection's tail split from
462	`pc.lowRank` and a column read out of the wrong plane is somebody else's
463	indexer query.
464	
465	**D14's boundary is now measurable twice inside one block.** The fused
466	[13952, 2560] projection is 35.7 MB at int8 and **17.9 at 4.5 bits**, so it
467	changes side of the 32 MiB MALL exactly as the DeltaNet's did; the output
468	[2560, 6144] projection is 15.7 and 7.9 and fits at every width, so it pays
469	only the unpack — and on the block's own ladder it is **1.00x at 128 tokens
470	and 1.04x slower at 512** while the block is faster overall. Four blocks, four
471	answers, one rule, and this is the first block that contains both of them.
472	
473	**The accuracy is the finding, and it is that this is the expensive family.**
474	`full_attn` alone is **4.0954 against 4.0289, +1.65%** over 145 chunks against
475	an eight-chunk screen of +1.05% — a fourth reading of L8c-4's warning, and the
476	second optimistic one. In percentage points per GB of decode token bought
477	back the four now read `deltanet` **0.87**, `hyper_conn` **0.93**, `lm_head`
478	**2.59** and `full_attn` **5.52**, so the shape is neither L8c-1's "inverse to
479	the bytes" nor L8c-6's "the two large ones are equal and the head is the
480	outlier" but **bimodal**, and the split is not size: the two families present
481	at 36 layers and 97 mixers cost ~0.9 pp/GB and the two present at 12 layers
482	and one matrix cost 2.6 and 5.5. **All four together are 4.1787, +3.72%,
483	against a sum of their four separate corpus deltas of 3.71%** — additivity to
484	0.01 pp, where the symmetric form compounded 11.7% into 18.5%.
485	
486	**And the fifth family closes D13's last open clause.** `qsa_indexer` is the
487	fused projection's fp16 tail — the model's only BF16 weights — and it costs
488	**0.51 bits a weight over the whole layer**, 11.3% of the block at 4.5 bits
489	where the same tail was 5.7% at int8. Naming it in the plan puts it on the
490	plane and the layer becomes **4.500 bits exactly**. Grading it took two
491	contexts. At n_ctx 2048 the quantised indexer is **bit-identical over all 145
492	chunks** — the per-chunk `nll` columns match to six decimals — because
493	`top_k + ratio - 1` is 2051, the selection names every cell and the score is
494	discarded, which is L8c-1's argument measured as an equality. At **n_ctx
495	2560**, where `selWidth` is 2051 of 2560 and the selection is dispatched, it
496	is **4.0723 to 4.0725 over 116 chunks: +0.005%, one part in forty of a
497	±0.0231 standard error** — with all 116 per-chunk rows differing, so the
498	narrower indexer really does select different cells and the corpus cannot
499	tell. **0.028 GB a token for +0.005%**, against `full_attn`'s 0.299 GB for
500	+1.65%. Decode with it is **31.51 tok/s**, the block 2.1 ms a token and
501	residency 79.85 GB.
502	
503	**What L8c-7 could not measure is not L8c-7's.** The obvious grading context
504	was 4096, and the whole-model graph does not complete above ~2560 rows: at 48
505	layers, in one staging, 2048 and 2560 tokens run at 1039 and 1091 tok/s and
506	3072 and 4096 never return — with no `LLM_DENSE_BANK` set and `-ppl` not
507	involved. The 4-layer prefix runs 4096 in 297 ms, `-ppl -ctx 4096` completes
508	at 4 and 12 layers, and the attention block alone at 4096 tokens in a

514	context is what this model is for.**

517	running total is 4.281 GB a token and +3.72%.** L8c-3's uniform asymmetric
518	plan projected 4.264 GB and a 56.7 tok/s ceiling; `lm_head`, `deltanet`,
519	`hyper_conn`, `full_attn` and `qsa_indexer` between them are **4.281 GB, a
520	56.5 tok/s ceiling and +3.72% measured over 145 chunks** — every asymmetric
521	plan measured still dominates L8c-1's recommendation on both axes at once,

532	already Q4_K and already the calibrated part of this checkpoint. §1.1's W4A8

**D14's hazard fires for the second time and is the smallest it has been**:
at ubatch 2048 the block is 1.02x slower, because its weights fit the 32 MiB
MALL at every width so the narrower bank adds only the unpack's ALU — 6 ms
of a 1921 ms pass, and the other three ubatches are faster. And **D12's
ladder did not move**: no rung's slab is a whole multiple of 4 KB on this
bank, so L7d's rule does not decide it, yet the spread is still 1.65x and
the winner is 32 as it was at int8.

**L8c-7 is the fourth family, and it needed nothing new.** The twelve
full-attention layers are 0.635 GB of a token, every matrix in the block is a
multiple of 256 wide, and `-DQ4B` already had every arm including the fp16
tail arm L8c-5 first exercised — so the stage is the wiring, and with it the
last of the two-valued `q8 bool` spelling (`q8Pipe`, `gemvPipe`,
`gemmBuilds`) leaves the package. **Decode is 30.05-30.11 tok/s to
31.41-31.57 — 1.25x llama.cpp — the block 3.5 ms a token to 2.3, a layer
57.94 MB to 32.22, residency 80.20 GB to 79.89, and prefill is faster at
every one of the four ubatches** (671.4 tok/s at 512 against 669.7, 1071.8 at
2048 against 1065.9). The bank is the format twice again — 97 664 projection
values and 17 920 output values identical to the same format through `sim.go`
on both arrangements of the tail, and chunk for chunk with the simulation over
eight chunks — plus a third check this family needed and the others did not,
because the decode GEMV has to derive the fused projection's tail split from
`pc.lowRank` and a column read out of the wrong plane is somebody else's
indexer query.

**D14's boundary is now measurable twice inside one block.** The fused
[13952, 2560] projection is 35.7 MB at int8 and **17.9 at 4.5 bits**, so it
changes side of the 32 MiB MALL exactly as the DeltaNet's did; the output
[2560, 6144] projection is 15.7 and 7.9 and fits at every width, so it pays
only the unpack — and on the block's own ladder it is **1.00x at 128 tokens
and 1.04x slower at 512** while the block is faster overall. Four blocks, four
answers, one rule, and this is the first block that contains both of them.

**The accuracy is the finding, and it is that this is the expensive family.**
`full_attn` alone is **4.0954 against 4.0289, +1.65%** over 145 chunks against
an eight-chunk screen of +1.05% — a fourth reading of L8c-4's warning, and the
second optimistic one. In percentage points per GB of decode token bought
back the four now read `deltanet` **0.87**, `hyper_conn` **0.93**, `lm_head`
**2.59** and `full_attn` **5.52**, so the shape is neither L8c-1's "inverse to
the bytes" nor L8c-6's "the two large ones are equal and the head is the
outlier" but **bimodal**, and the split is not size: the two families present
at 36 layers and 97 mixers cost ~0.9 pp/GB and the two present at 12 layers
and one matrix cost 2.6 and 5.5. **All four together are 4.1787, +3.72%,
against a sum of their four separate corpus deltas of 3.71%** — additivity to
0.01 pp, where the symmetric form compounded 11.7% into 18.5%.

**And the fifth family closes D13's last open clause.** `qsa_indexer` is the
fused projection's fp16 tail — the model's only BF16 weights — and it costs
**0.51 bits a weight over the whole layer**, 11.3% of the block at 4.5 bits
where the same tail was 5.7% at int8. Naming it in the plan puts it on the
plane and the layer becomes **4.500 bits exactly**. Grading it took two
contexts. At n_ctx 2048 the quantised indexer is **bit-identical over all 145
chunks** — the per-chunk `nll` columns match to six decimals — because
`top_k + ratio - 1` is 2051, the selection names every cell and the score is
discarded, which is L8c-1's argument measured as an equality. At **n_ctx
2560**, where `selWidth` is 2051 of 2560 and the selection is dispatched, it
is **4.0723 to 4.0725 over 116 chunks: +0.005%, one part in forty of a
±0.0231 standard error** — with all 116 per-chunk rows differing, so the
narrower indexer really does select different cells and the corpus cannot
tell. **0.028 GB a token for +0.005%**, against `full_attn`'s 0.299 GB for
+1.65%. Decode with it is **31.51 tok/s**, the block 2.1 ms a token and
residency 79.85 GB.

**What L8c-7 could not measure is not L8c-7's.** The obvious grading context
was 4096, and the whole-model graph does not complete above ~2560 rows: at 48
layers, in one staging, 2048 and 2560 tokens run at 1039 and 1091 tok/s and
3072 and 4096 never return — with no `LLM_DENSE_BANK` set and `-ppl` not
involved. The 4-layer prefix runs 4096 in 297 ms, `-ppl -ctx 4096` completes
at 4 and 12 layers, and the attention block alone at 4096 tokens in a
4096-cell cache with the selection live is 325 ms for twelve layers — so
neither the block nor the selection is implicated. A `SIGQUIT` puts the stall
in `Graph.flush → recorder.submit`, in `[syscall]`, one thread at 100% of a
core with the GPU at 2-3% and the shim's own 20-second fence timeout never
firing. **It is the open question this stage hands over, because a long
context is what this model is for.**

**The plan was 4.50 bits at +4.24%, and five families in, the measured
running total is 4.281 GB a token and +3.72%.** L8c-3's uniform asymmetric
plan projected 4.264 GB and a 56.7 tok/s ceiling; `lm_head`, `deltanet`,
`hyper_conn`, `full_attn` and `qsa_indexer` between them are **4.281 GB, a
56.5 tok/s ceiling and +3.72% measured over 145 chunks** — every asymmetric
plan measured still dominates L8c-1's recommendation on both axes at once,
and the four corpus deltas add rather than compound. **One family is left**:
`ple_proj`, the PLE block's fused key/value projection, 0.033 B parameters run
**once** at layer 1 — 0.017 GB a token, and the one block in this vertical
that never got L8a's int8 bank either, so it is two bank stages in one.

**After it, the bank is not where the decode time is, and has not been since
L8c-5**: 31.5 tok/s measured against a 56.5 ceiling is 56%. What is left on
that side is the two things the simulation cannot reach — the F32 router at
fp16 (+1.5 tok/s of ceiling) and the 512 expert banks at ~4.25 (+3.0), which
are 1.504 GB of every token and 35% of what a step now reads, and which are
already Q4_K and already the calibrated part of this checkpoint. §1.1's W4A8
layout stays open beside all of it: it is a *symmetric* weight and an
int8-activation one, where every rung built here multiplies an fp16 A, and an
asymmetric version folds the min into the epilogue as a per-group correction
times the activation's column sum — one extra reduction over A and no change
to the matrix core. And **the graph does not complete above ~2560 rows at 48
layers**, which is the one open item that is not about a width. Past all of it
is **phase 3**, where MTP speculation is worth 1.5-1.8x and batching amortises
the dense half completely.

11	// stack — 21 MB at 512 tokens, out of an arena that reads at 0.2 GB/s.
12	//
13	// What is not on the device is the gather itself, and that is D2 rather than
14	// an omission: `per_layer_token_embd` is 28.80 GB of IQ4_NL, a quarter of the
15	// whole checkpoint, and a token reads sixteen rows of 160 values out of it —
16	// 1.41 KB. It stays in the host mapping, the sixteen rows are hashed and
17	// gathered on the CPU (PLERows, Model.PLEGather), and what crosses to the
18	// device is the [T][2560] result. llama.cpp does exactly this, with
19	// `TENSOR_READ_LAZY` and a host-built row index.
20	//
21	// Arenas are this type's own. At L6, where the whole stack is resident, they
22	// merge with HCGPU's — which is why both share one binding contract and one
23	// push-constant block (shaders/llm_common.glsl) even though neither uses all
24	// of it.
25	
26	import (
27		"fmt"
28		"math"
29		"time"
30		"unsafe"
31	
32		"strix-halo-vulkan/shaders"
33		"strix-halo-vulkan/vk"
34	)
35	
36	// pleKVBN is the compiled column block of the fused key/value projection,
37	// which is the plain arm of shaders/llm_gemm.comp. The row block is a ladder,
38	// because this dispatch is bound by the *weight*: B is 65.5 MB of fp16,
39	// twice the 32 MiB MALL, so a workgroup carrying BM token rows reads all of
40	// it M/BM times — 1.05 GB at 512 tokens with BM=32, and 262 MB with BM=128.
41	const pleKVBN = 64
42	
43	// PLEKernel names one build of the fused projection, by its row block.
44	type PLEKernel string
45	
46	const (
47		PLEKVM2 PLEKernel = "kv_m2"
48		PLEKVM4 PLEKernel = "kv_m4"
49		PLEKVM8 PLEKernel = "kv_m8"
50	)
51	
52	type pleVariant struct {
53		name  PLEKernel
54		spirv []byte
55		bm    int
56	}
57	
58	var pleVariants = []pleVariant{
59		{PLEKVM2, shaders.LLMGEMMPlainM2, 32},
60		{PLEKVM4, shaders.LLMGEMMPlainM4, 64},
61		{PLEKVM8, shaders.LLMGEMMPlainM8, 128},
62	}
63	
64	// PLEKernels lists the rungs, narrowest first.
65	func PLEKernels() []PLEKernel { return []PLEKernel{PLEKVM2, PLEKVM4, PLEKVM8} }
66	
67	// PLEKernelFor is the measured schedule (research/l2d-ple.md). The rung is
68	// chosen against the *weight*: at 512 tokens BM=32/64/128 cost 2643/1611/1382
69	// us and at 2048 they cost 16995/7848/5177 — a 3.3x spread, which is the
70	// weight read M/BM times and nothing else. Below ~128 tokens there are not
71	// enough rows to fill a BM of 128 and the ladder turns over.
72	func PLEKernelFor(tokens int) PLEKernel {
73		if tokens <= 128 {
74			return PLEKVM4
75		}
76		return PLEKVM8
77	}
78	
79	// DefaultPLEKernel is what a block runs before Upload has said how long the
80	// prompt is.
81	func DefaultPLEKernel() PLEKernel { return PLEKVM8 }
82	
83	func pleVariantFor(k PLEKernel) (pleVariant, bool) {
84		for _, v := range pleVariants {
85			if v.name == k {
86				return v, true
87			}
88		}
89		return pleVariant{}, false
90	}

92	// PLEOpts are the choices that change what the block allocates.
93	type PLEOpts struct {
94		// ConvOut makes the convolution write silu(conv) as well as adding it
95		// into the residual, so it can be checked against `ple_conv_out-N`. The
96		// residual add does not need the tensor; the trace comparison does.
97		ConvOut bool
98	}
99	
100	// PLEGPU runs the n-gram block for one layer.
101	type PLEGPU struct {
102		// rec, when set, collects this block's dispatches into the pass's one
103		// command buffer instead of submitting them (record.go).
104		rec *recorder
105		dev *vk.Device
106		cfg PLEConfig
107	
108		wbuf, abuf, hbuf, bank *vk.Buffer
109		pipes                  map[string]*vk.ComputePipeline
110		mods                   []*vk.ShaderModule
111	
112		tokens, arenaRows, rows int
113		lda                     int
114		kv                      PLEKernel
115		// autoKernel re-chooses the rung per run, using PLEKernelFor. SetKernel
116		// turns it off, because a caller that named a rung meant it.
117		autoKernel bool
118	
119		// fp32 weights: the three norms and the depthwise kernel.
120		wNormKey, wNormQuery, wNormConv, wConv uint32
121		// fp32 activations.
122		aRes, aKV, aGate, aGated, aNorm, aConvOut uint32
123		// aHist is the convolution's ring: (Conv-1)*NGram rows of the normed
124		// gated value, addressed by **position** modulo its length, and the only
125		// tensor in this block that outlives a run (L7b).
126		aHist    uint32
127		actElems int
128		// past is how many tokens of this sequence are already behind the run,
129		// which is how far back the convolution may reach. Zero is a fresh
130		// sequence, where anything before token 0 is zero.
131		past int
132		// fp16 activations: the gathered n-gram embedding, the GEMM's A operand.
133		hEmb   uint32
134		hElems int
135	
136		convOut bool
137	}
138	
139	// kvN is the fused projection's output width: the wide key and the n_embd
140	// value in one matrix, because they read the same gathered embedding — the
141	// same argument that puts `inject` on the hyper-connection block's down
142	// projection.
143	func (g *PLEGPU) kvN() int { return roundUpInt(g.cfg.Wide()+g.cfg.NEmbd, pleKVBN) }
144	
145	// NewPLEGPU stages one layer's n-gram block onto the device.
146	func NewPLEGPU(dev *vk.Device, cfg PLEConfig, maxTokens int, w PLEWeights, opts PLEOpts) (*PLEGPU, error) {
147		if maxTokens <= 0 {
148			return nil, fmt.Errorf("llm: maxTokens is %d", maxTokens)
149		}
150		if cfg.NEmbd%coopMatTile != 0 || cfg.EmbdWidth() != cfg.NEmbd {
151			return nil, fmt.Errorf("llm: the fused key/value projection assumes %d heads of %d make n_embd %d",
152				cfg.NHeads, cfg.HeadDim, cfg.NEmbd)
153		}
154		ok, err := canWMMA(dev)
155		if err != nil {
156			return nil, err
157		}
158		if !ok {
159			return nil, fmt.Errorf("llm: this device has no 16x16x16 fp16 cooperative matrix")
160		}
161		g := &PLEGPU{
162			dev: dev, cfg: cfg,
163			pipes:      make(map[string]*vk.ComputePipeline),
164			tokens:     maxTokens,
165			rows:       maxTokens,
166			lda:        cfg.NEmbd + gemmPad,
167			convOut:    opts.ConvOut,
168			kv:         DefaultPLEKernel(),
169			autoKernel: true,
170		}
171		align := 1
172		for _, v := range pleVariants {
173			align = maxInt(align, v.bm)
174		}
175		g.arenaRows = roundUpInt(maxTokens, align)
176		if err := g.alloc(); err != nil {
177			g.Destroy()
178			return nil, err
179		}
180		if err := g.build(); err != nil {
181			g.Destroy()
182			return nil, err
183		}
184		if err := g.stage(w); err != nil {
185			g.Destroy()
186			return nil, err
187		}
188		return g, nil
189	}
190	
191	func (g *PLEGPU) alloc() error {
192		c := g.cfg
193		wide, rows := c.Wide(), g.arenaRows
194	
195		total32 := 3*wide + wide*c.Conv
196		var err error
197		if g.wbuf, err = g.dev.NewBuffer(total32 * 4); err != nil {
198			return fmt.Errorf("llm: PLE fp32 weight arena: %w", err)
199		}
200		g.wNormKey = 0
201		g.wNormQuery = uint32(wide)
202		g.wNormConv = uint32(2 * wide)
203		g.wConv = uint32(3 * wide)
204	
205		alloc := func(n int) uint32 {
206			off := uint32(g.actElems)
207			g.actElems += (n + 63) &^ 63
208			return off
209		}
210		// The sequence position, and it must be the arena's dword 0: the kernels
211		// read it as `actu[0]` (SEQ_PAST in llm_common.glsl, P1c). SetPast writes
212		// it.
213		if seq := alloc(1); seq != 0 {
214			return fmt.Errorf("llm: the sequence slot is at %d, and SEQ_PAST is actu[0]", seq)
215		}
216		g.aRes = alloc(rows * wide)
217		g.aKV = alloc(rows * g.kvN())
218		g.aGated = alloc(rows * wide)
219		g.aNorm = alloc(rows * wide)
220		g.aGate = alloc(rows * c.HC)
221		// 9 rows of 10240 floats — 368 KB — against the 168 MB a whole context's
222		// worth of `aNorm` would be, which is the other way to let a tap reach
223		// behind the run.
224		g.aHist = alloc(c.ConvHist() * wide)
225		g.aConvOut = noW
226		if g.convOut {
227			g.aConvOut = alloc(rows * wide)
228		}
229		if g.abuf, err = newArena(g.dev, g.actElems*4); err != nil {
230			return fmt.Errorf("llm: PLE fp32 activation arena (%d MB): %w", (g.actElems*4)>>20, err)
231		}
232	
233		g.hEmb = 0
234		g.hElems = rows * g.lda
235		if g.hbuf, err = newArena(g.dev, g.hElems*2); err != nil {
236			return fmt.Errorf("llm: PLE fp16 activation arena: %w", err)
237		}
238		// Zeroed once: the A operand's pad columns and a short run's pad rows.
239		g.hbuf.Zero()
240		g.abuf.Zero()
241	
242		if g.bank, err = g.dev.NewBuffer(g.kvN() * c.NEmbd * 2); err != nil {
243			return fmt.Errorf("llm: PLE fp16 weight bank (%d MB): %w", (g.kvN()*c.NEmbd*2)>>20, err)
244		}
245		return nil
246	}
247	
248	func (g *PLEGPU) build() error {
249		bufs := []*vk.Buffer{g.wbuf, g.abuf, g.hbuf, g.bank, g.abuf}
250		pcSize := uint32(unsafe.Sizeof(push{}))
251		feat := g.dev.Features()
252		sgs, err := g.dev.Physical().SubgroupSizeControl()
253		if err != nil {
254			return fmt.Errorf("llm: subgroup size control: %w", err)
255		}
256		if !feat.SubgroupSizeControl || !sgs.Supported || sgs.MaxSubgroupSize < 64 {
257			return fmt.Errorf("llm: the GEMM rung needs a pinned 64-wide subgroup")
258		}
259		for name, spirv := range map[string][]byte{
260			"gate": shaders.LLMPLEGate,
261			"conv": shaders.LLMPLEConv,
262			"hist": shaders.LLMSeqHist,
263		} {
264			if err := g.pipeline(name, spirv, vk.PipelineSpec{Buffers: bufs, PushConstantSize: pcSize}); err != nil {
265				return err
266			}
267		}
268		for _, v := range pleVariants {
269			if err := g.pipeline(string(v.name), v.spirv, vk.PipelineSpec{
270				Buffers: bufs, PushConstantSize: pcSize, RequiredSubgroupSize: 64,
271			}); err != nil {
272				return err
273			}
274		}
275		return nil
276	}
277	
278	func (g *PLEGPU) pipeline(name string, spirv []byte, spec vk.PipelineSpec) error {
279		mod, err := g.dev.NewShaderModule(spirv)
280		if err != nil {
281			return fmt.Errorf("llm: shader ple.%s: %w", name, err)
282		}
283		g.mods = append(g.mods, mod)
284		pipe, err := g.dev.NewPipeline(mod, spec)
285		if err != nil {
286			return fmt.Errorf("llm: pipeline ple.%s: %w", name, err)
287		}
288		g.pipes[name] = pipe
289		return nil
290	}

292	// stage packs the block's weights: the three norms and the depthwise kernel
293	// as fp32, and the key and value projections as one fragment-tiled matrix.
294	func (g *PLEGPU) stage(w PLEWeights) error {
295		c := g.cfg
296		wide := c.Wide()
297		for _, t := range []struct {
298			name string
299			off  uint32
300			src  []float32
301			want int
302		}{
303			{"norm_key", g.wNormKey, w.NormKey, wide},
304			{"norm_query", g.wNormQuery, w.NormQuery, wide},
305			{"norm_conv", g.wNormConv, w.NormConv, wide},
306			{"conv1d", g.wConv, w.Conv1d, wide * c.Conv},
307		} {
308			if len(t.src) != t.want {
309				return fmt.Errorf("llm: ple_%s is %d values, want %d", t.name, len(t.src), t.want)
310			}
311			g.wbuf.WriteFloat32At(int(t.off), t.src)
312		}
313		if len(w.Key) != wide*c.NEmbd {
314			return fmt.Errorf("llm: ple_key is %d values, want %d", len(w.Key), wide*c.NEmbd)
315		}
316		if len(w.Value) != c.NEmbd*c.NEmbd {
317			return fmt.Errorf("llm: ple_value is %d values, want %d", len(w.Value), c.NEmbd*c.NEmbd)
318		}
319		// Key rows first, then value's: the gate kernel reads the value at column
320		// `wide` of the same row, which is what makes this one dispatch.
321		buf := make([]uint16, g.kvN()*c.NEmbd)
322		tileB(buf, w.Key, wide, c.NEmbd, func(i int) int { return i })
323		tileB(buf, w.Value, c.NEmbd, c.NEmbd, func(i int) int { return wide + i })
324		g.bank.WriteUint16At(0, buf)
325		return nil
326	}

328	// SetKernel chooses the fused projection's rung. Every rung is built and they
329	// all read the same staged weight, so this moves a pipeline and nothing else.
330	func (g *PLEGPU) SetKernel(k PLEKernel) error {
331		if _, ok := pleVariantFor(k); !ok {
332			return fmt.Errorf("llm: no PLE kernel %q (have %v)", k, PLEKernels())
333		}
334		g.kv = k
335		g.autoKernel = false
336		return nil
337	}
338	
339	// Kernel reports the rung in use.
340	func (g *PLEGPU) Kernel() PLEKernel { return g.kv }
341	
342	// Upload writes a run's inputs: the wide residual this block adds into, and
343	// the gathered n-gram embedding, [T][NHeads*HeadDim], which the host produced
344	// from the mmap'd table.
345	func (g *PLEGPU) Upload(res, embd []float32, nTok int) error {
346		c := g.cfg
347		if nTok <= 0 || nTok > g.tokens {
348			return fmt.Errorf("llm: %d tokens, arenas are built for %d", nTok, g.tokens)
349		}
350		if len(res) != nTok*c.Wide() {
351			return fmt.Errorf("llm: residual is %d values, want %d", len(res), nTok*c.Wide())
352		}
353		if len(embd) != nTok*c.EmbdWidth() {
354			return fmt.Errorf("llm: embedding is %d values, want %d", len(embd), nTok*c.EmbdWidth())
355		}
356		g.rows = nTok
357		if g.autoKernel {
358			g.kv = PLEKernelFor(nTok)
359		}
360		g.abuf.WriteFloat32At(int(g.aRes), res)
361		slab := make([]uint16, nTok*g.lda)
362		narrowRows(slab, embd, nTok, c.EmbdWidth(), g.lda)
363		g.hbuf.WriteUint16At(int(g.hEmb), slab)
364		return nil
365	}
366	
367	// graph is the block's three dispatches, with a label each.
368	func (g *PLEGPU) graph() ([]vk.MultiDispatch, []string) {
369		c := g.cfg
370		wide := c.Wide()
371		base := push{
372			ResOff: g.aRes, XnOff: g.hEmb, GammaOff: g.wNormKey, GateOff: g.aGate,
373			Tokens: uint32(g.rows), NEmbd: uint32(c.NEmbd), HC: uint32(c.HC),
374			LDA: uint32(g.lda), Eps: math.Float32bits(c.Eps),
375			KVOff: g.aKV, GatedOff: g.aGated, NormOff: g.aNorm,
376			ConvOff: g.wConv, ConvOutOff: g.aConvOut,
377			GammaQOff: g.wNormQuery, GammaCOff: g.wNormConv,
378			Kern: uint32(c.Conv), Dil: uint32(c.NGram),
379			GemmN: uint32(g.kvN()),
380			// SEQ_HIST: a field this block does not otherwise use, because the
381			// push block is full at 64 uints (llm_common.glsl). The position is
382			// not here any more: SEQ_PAST is dword 0 of the arena (P1c), written
383			// by SetPast, so `lowRank` stays zero and the dispatch is
384			// byte-identical every decode step.
385			InjOff: g.aHist,
386		}
387	
388		var d []vk.MultiDispatch
389		var kinds []string
390		add := func(pipe, kind string, gx, gy uint32, pc push) {
391			d = append(d, vk.MultiDispatch{Pipeline: g.pipes[pipe], GroupsX: gx, GroupsY: gy, PushConstants: pc.bytes()})
392			kinds = append(kinds, kind)
393		}
394	
395		v, _ := pleVariantFor(g.kv)
396		kv := base
397		kv.OutOff = g.aKV
398		kv.GemmM, kv.GemmK = uint32(roundUpInt(g.rows, v.bm)), uint32(c.NEmbd)
399		add(string(g.kv), "kv", uint32(g.kvN()/pleKVBN), uint32(roundUpInt(g.rows, v.bm)/v.bm), kv)
400	
401		add("gate", "gate", uint32(c.HC), uint32(g.rows), base)
402		add("conv", "conv", uint32((wide+255)/256), uint32(g.rows), base)
403		// The ring, for whatever runs next. It is the only dispatch here that a
404		// single-shot prefill does not need, and it is nine rows.
405		hist := base
406		hist.LoOff = g.aNorm // SEQ_SRC
407		hist.GemmM, hist.GemmK = uint32(c.ConvHist()), uint32(wide)
408		add("hist", "hist", uint32((wide+255)/256), uint32(minInt(g.rows, c.ConvHist())), hist)
409		return d, kinds
410	}
411	
412	// Past is how many tokens of this sequence precede the next run, SetPast moves
413	// it, and Reset starts a fresh sequence.
414	//
415	// Nothing is cleared on a reset: the convolution masks every tap that reaches
416	// before position zero, so the ring's contents are unreachable rather than
417	// merely stale.
418	func (g *PLEGPU) Past() int { return g.past }
419	func (g *PLEGPU) Reset()    { g.past = 0; g.writeSeq() }
420	
421	// SetPast places the next run's first token at position n.
422	func (g *PLEGPU) SetPast(n int) error {
423		if n < 0 {
424			return fmt.Errorf("llm: position %d", n)
425		}
426		g.past = n
427		g.writeSeq()
428		return nil
429	}
430	
431	// writeSeq puts the position where the kernels read it: dword 0 of the fp32
432	// arena (SEQ_PAST in llm_common.glsl), a host write instead of a push
433	// constant so the recorded decode step is byte-identical every token (P1c).
434	func (g *PLEGPU) writeSeq() { g.abuf.WriteUint32At(0, []uint32{uint32(g.past)}) }
435	
436	// Run executes the block over whatever Upload left in the arenas. The
437	// residual is updated in place.
438	func (g *PLEGPU) Run() error {
439		d, kinds := g.graph()
440		// One command buffer for the whole block, not one a dispatch: a submit
441		// and a fence wait is ~150 us here and a decode step is a batch of one,
442		// so what the sequence costs is how many times it is handed over
443		// (LLM.md L7c). And when the graph is recording a whole pass, not even
444		// one a block (L7d).
445		if g.rec.add(ownPLE, kinds, d) {
446			return nil
447		}
448		if _, err := vk.DispatchMultiTimed(d, 1, 1, true); err != nil {
449			return fmt.Errorf("llm: ple, %d dispatches (%v): %w", len(d), kinds, err)
450		}
451		return nil
452	}
453	
454	// Profile times each dispatch on the GPU over iters back-to-back runs. The
455	// residual is read and written by the last one, so a repeated dispatch is not
456	// idempotent — this measures cost, not a result.
457	func (g *PLEGPU) Profile(iters int) ([]Stage, error) {
458		if iters <= 0 {
459			iters = 1
460		}
461		d, kinds := g.graph()
462		out := make([]Stage, 0, len(d))
463		for i := range d {
464			dur, err := vk.DispatchMultiTimed(d[i:i+1], 1, uint32(iters), true)
465			if err != nil {
466				return out, fmt.Errorf("llm: ple dispatch %d (%s): %w", i, kinds[i], err)
467			}
468			out = append(out, Stage{Kind: kinds[i], GPU: dur / time.Duration(iters)})
469		}
470		return out, nil
471	}

473	// The tensors a run leaves behind, in the CPU reference's layout.
474	
475	// Res is the wide residual after the block added into it, [T][hc*nEmbd].
476	func (g *PLEGPU) Res() []float32 { return g.abuf.ReadFloat32At(int(g.aRes), g.rows*g.cfg.Wide()) }
477	
478	// Gate is the per-stream scalar gate, [T][hc].
479	func (g *PLEGPU) Gate() []float32 { return g.abuf.ReadFloat32At(int(g.aGate), g.rows*g.cfg.HC) }
480	
481	// Gated is the value vector scaled by it, [T][hc*nEmbd].
482	func (g *PLEGPU) Gated() []float32 { return g.abuf.ReadFloat32At(int(g.aGated), g.rows*g.cfg.Wide()) }
483	
484	// ConvOut is silu(conv), and is empty unless the block was built to write it.
485	func (g *PLEGPU) ConvOut() []float32 {
486		if !g.convOut {
487			return nil
488		}
489		return g.abuf.ReadFloat32At(int(g.aConvOut), g.rows*g.cfg.Wide())
490	}

492	// Key and Value are the fused projection's two halves, for a failure that
493	// needs locating upstream of the gate.
494	func (g *PLEGPU) Key() []float32   { return g.kvSlice(0, g.cfg.Wide()) }
495	func (g *PLEGPU) Value() []float32 { return g.kvSlice(g.cfg.Wide(), g.cfg.NEmbd) }
496	
497	func (g *PLEGPU) kvSlice(col, width int) []float32 {
498		raw := g.abuf.ReadFloat32At(int(g.aKV), g.rows*g.kvN())
499		out := make([]float32, g.rows*width)
500		for t := 0; t < g.rows; t++ {
501			copy(out[t*width:(t+1)*width], raw[t*g.kvN()+col:])
502		}
503		return out
504	}

506	// WeightBytes is what the block costs on the device and ActivationBytes what
507	// its arenas cost.
508	func (g *PLEGPU) WeightBytes() int { return g.wbuf.Size() + g.bank.Size() }
509	
510	// Buffers is how many device allocations the block holds. L6a counts them
511	// across the whole model: `maxStorageBufferRange` is 4 GiB - 4 here, so the
512	// number is a residency fact and not bookkeeping.
513	func (g *PLEGPU) Buffers() int         { return 4 }
514	func (g *PLEGPU) ActivationBytes() int { return g.abuf.Size() + g.hbuf.Size() }

516	// Destroy releases every Vulkan object.
517	func (g *PLEGPU) Destroy() {
518		for _, p := range g.pipes {
519			p.Destroy()
520		}
521		for _, m := range g.mods {
522			m.Destroy()
523		}
524		for _, b := range []*vk.Buffer{g.hbuf, g.abuf, g.wbuf, g.bank} {
525			if b != nil {
526				b.Destroy()
527			}
528		}
529	}
530	
531	// ResPort is the wide residual this block adds into: fp32 [T][hc*nEmbd], read
532	// and written in place. It is the only tensor of the PLE block that crosses a
533	// boundary — the gathered n-gram embedding comes from the host, because the
534	// 28.80 GB table it is gathered from never reaches the device (D2).
535	func (g *PLEGPU) ResPort() Port {
536		return Port{Buf: g.abuf, Off: g.aRes, Stride: g.cfg.Wide(), Width: g.cfg.Wide(), Rows: g.rows}
537	}
538	
539	// UploadEmbd writes the gathered n-gram embedding alone, for a caller that is
540	// filling the residual with a Move rather than an Upload.
541	func (g *PLEGPU) UploadEmbd(embd []float32, nTok int) error {
542		c := g.cfg
543		if nTok <= 0 || nTok > g.tokens {
544			return fmt.Errorf("llm: %d tokens, arenas are built for %d", nTok, g.tokens)
545		}
546		if len(embd) != nTok*c.EmbdWidth() {
547			return fmt.Errorf("llm: embedding is %d values, want %d", len(embd), nTok*c.EmbdWidth())
548		}
549		g.rows = nTok
550		if g.autoKernel {
551			g.kv = PLEKernelFor(nTok)
552		}
553		slab := make([]uint16, nTok*g.lda)
554		narrowRows(slab, embd, nTok, c.EmbdWidth(), g.lda)
555		g.hbuf.WriteUint16At(int(g.hEmb), slab)
556		return nil
557	}

356	// DensePlan is the simulation this process runs, from LLM_DENSE_SIM plus the
357	// two scope variables. It is read once, and a bad spec is fatal rather than
358	// ignored: a run that silently measured the wrong bank would be worse than
359	// one that did not start.
360	//
361	//	LLM_DENSE_SIM=q4_0/32                        every streamed dense family
362	//	LLM_DENSE_SIM=deltanet=q4_0/32,lm_head=q5sym/32   a width per family
363	//	LLM_DENSE_SIM_FAMILIES=deltanet,lm_head      restrict a single-width spec
364	//	LLM_DENSE_SIM_SRC=tail                       only what the checkpoint
365	//	                                             does not ship as Q8_0
366	func DensePlan() QuantPlan {
367		denseSimOnce.Do(func() {
368			p, err := ParseQuantPlan(os.Getenv("LLM_DENSE_SIM"),
369				os.Getenv("LLM_DENSE_SIM_FAMILIES"), os.Getenv("LLM_DENSE_SIM_SRC"),
370				os.Getenv("LLM_DENSE_SIM_QUANT"))
371			if err != nil {
372				panic(err)
373			}
374			densePlan = p
375		})
376		return densePlan
377	}
378	
379	var (
380		denseBankOnce sync.Once
381		denseBankPlan QuantPlan
382	)
383	
384	// DenseBankPlan is which dense families are staged on **the real 4.5-bit
385	// bank** (bank_q4.go), from `LLM_DENSE_BANK` — the same grammar `LLM_DENSE_SIM`
386	// takes, and `LLM_DENSE_BANK_QUANT` beside it, because a plan is a plan
387	// whether it is simulated or built.
388	//
389	//	LLM_DENSE_BANK=lm_head=q4_k/32              the family L8c-4 has a kernel for
390	//	LLM_DENSE_BANK_QUANT=imatrix                the default; rtn is the control
391	//
392	// It defaults to `imatrix` where `LLM_DENSE_SIM` defaults to `rtn`, and that
393	// is deliberate: a simulation's default arm is the one every L8c-1 rung was
394	// measured with, where a *bank*'s is the one L8c-3 recommends building
395	// (+4.24% against the calibrated symmetric form's +15.63%). A family the
396	// matrix does not cover falls back to round-to-nearest the way ggml does.
397	//
398	// The two are separate variables and a run that sets both is measuring
399	// something incoherent — a weight quantised twice — so `-ppl` and the graph
400	// refuse it rather than average it.
401	func DenseBankPlan() QuantPlan {
402		denseBankOnce.Do(func() {
403			mode := os.Getenv("LLM_DENSE_BANK_QUANT")
404			if strings.TrimSpace(mode) == "" {
405				mode = "imatrix"
406			}
407			p, err := ParseQuantPlan(os.Getenv("LLM_DENSE_BANK"), "", "", mode)
408			if err != nil {
409				panic(err)
410			}
411			if !p.Off() && !DensePlan().Off() {
412				panic(fmt.Errorf("llm: LLM_DENSE_BANK=%s and LLM_DENSE_SIM=%s would quantise the same weight twice",
413					p, DensePlan()))
414			}
415			denseBankPlan = p
416		})
417		return denseBankPlan
418	}
419	
420	// ApplyTo round-trips one staged weight through the plan, if the plan covers
421	// it, and records what it touched.
422	//
423	// It is the single entry point both staging paths use — `Model.F32` for
424	// everything and `gpu_head.go` for the lm head, which is too big to reach the
425	// device as floats — because the two behaving differently is exactly the bug
426	// L8c-1 found. x is [n][k] row-major, which is ggml's own order for a weight
427	// stated [k, n].
428	func (p QuantPlan) ApplyTo(name string, q8Source bool, x []float32, k int) error {
429		q, ok := p.For(name, q8Source)
430		if !ok {
431			return nil
432		}
433		var qw []float32
434		if q.Mode == "imatrix" {
435			im, err := DefaultImatrix()
436			if err != nil {
437				return err
438			}
439			if qw, err = im.Columns(name); err != nil {
440				return fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", name, err)
441			}
442			if qw == nil {
443				// **The published matrix has no entry for this tensor**, which
444				// is not a failure and is not rare: unsloth's covers `blk.N.*`
445				// only, so `output.weight` and the head mixer's two projections
446				// — 0.636 B weights, 14% of a dense token — have no calibration
447				// data at all.
448				//
449				// ggml does exactly this: `quantize_row_q4_0_impl` returns
450				// `quantize_row_q4_0_ref` when `quant_weights` is null, so an
451				// uncovered tensor is round-to-nearest. Following it keeps the
452				// simulation's arms comparable to a real `llama-quantize`, and
453				// the tally below is what stops that being invisible — a plan
454				// that is half calibrated has to say so.
455				q.Mode = "rtn"
456				simCountUncal(name, len(x))
457			}
458		}
459		if err := q.ApplyWeighted(x, k, qw); err != nil {
460			return fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", name, err)
461		}
462		simCount(name, len(x))
463		return nil
464	}
465	
466	// imatrixCols is the published importance row for a tensor, or nil — which is
467	// both "this mode does not calibrate" and "the matrix has no entry for this
468	// tensor", because ggml treats the second as the first
469	// (`quantize_row_q4_K_impl` falls back to `_ref` on a null `quant_weights`)
470	// and so does everything here.
471	//
472	// It is `ApplyTo`'s lookup as a function, because L8c-4's *bank* needs the
473	// same row the *simulation* used and the two reading different matrices would
474	// be the bug this file was written to avoid.
475	func imatrixCols(name, mode string) ([]float32, error) {
476		if mode != "imatrix" && mode != "imatrix+gain" {
477			return nil, nil
478		}
479		im, err := DefaultImatrix()
480		if err != nil {
481			return nil, err
482		}
483		qw, err := im.Columns(name)
484		if err != nil {
485			return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: %w", name, err)
486		}
487		return qw, nil
488	}

1188		if i := strings.Index(name, "."); i >= 0 && strings.HasPrefix(name, "blk.") {
1189			if j := strings.Index(name[i+1:], "."); j >= 0 {
1190				base = name[i+1+j+1:]
1191			}
1192		}

1194		case "hc_attn_down.weight", "hc_attn_up.weight", "hc_attn_inject.weight",
1195			"hc_ffn_down.weight", "hc_ffn_up.weight", "hc_ffn_inject.weight":
1196			return "hyper_conn"
1197		case "attn_q.weight", "attn_k.weight", "attn_v.weight":
1198			return "full_attn"
1199		case "attn_output.weight":
1200			return "full_attn"
1201		case "indexer.q_proj.weight", "indexer.k_proj.weight":
1202			return "qsa_indexer"
1203		case "attn_qkv.weight", "attn_gate.weight", "ssm_out.weight":
1204			return "deltanet"
1205		case "ssm_alpha.weight", "ssm_beta.weight":
1206			return "deltanet"
1207		}
1208		switch base {

1214			return "ple_proj"

   (The item that used to stand here — "explain the down projection's 198 GB/s
   against gate_up's 235" — is **done**: it is a fixed cost per output row
   inside the wave, 19.8% of down's time against -0.4% of gate_up's, and the
   N block takes down to 98% of gate_up's rate. Dividing the workgroup count
   alone is worth 1.02x, so the grid was never it. See IDEAS §1.10. The item
   *before* that one — "carry §3.5's stride window back to the GEMV kernels" —
   is also done and came out backwards: at constant traffic the *unpadded* bank
   wins at both shapes, including down's gcd-64 row, and every pad costs
   1.12-2.4x. The window is a tiled-read rule. See §1.8 finding 6 and §5.1b
   rule 1's second amendment.)

4. **`VEC=32` is retired.** Left here so it is not re-proposed: the largest
   reduction length any of the five models decodes over is 6144, and at
   6144 every built width already reads the bus. There is no matrix for it.
5. **The two inverted cells in §3.5.** `moe.gate_up` at 8192 tokens in
   `reg32_bt_hkab4` and `reg16x32_bt_hkab4_w32`: the *grouped* dispatch is
   0.74-0.75x the per-expert loop, reproducibly across three runs, where
   every other cell goes the other way and the occupancy story predicts a
   tie. Both are the narrow-BN kernels at the largest dispatch (51k and 102k
   workgroups). Small, and the only cell in `moe` that the attribution gets
   backwards.
6. **Finish §2.7's ladder on the other winners.** It was run on `reg64_bt`
   and `reg32_bt` only. `reg64x128` and `wg128x256` are the AI-43/85 shapes
   and already sit at 252 VGPRs with 32 accumulators, so they cannot hoist as
   they stand — whether the lever survives into them is what says how it
   composes with arithmetic intensity. §6.2 has now closed off the wave32
   route to that: the register ceiling halves with the wave, so a
   32-accumulator variant spills at wave32 rather than gaining headroom.
   Also missing: a row-major `hkb4`, which completes the 2x2 of (operand
   hoisted) x (layout) that §2.7 could only half-fill, and an explanation for
   the one reproducible cell where padding *hurts* (`reg32_bt_hkab4`, 0.88x).
7. **The MALL's own slice structure — still open, and now with one more
   clue.** Under partial channel coverage the MALL keeps a working set only
   while its *span* is also inside 32 MiB, one case lands halfway, and the
   traversal axis has added MALL cells the coverage law fits (2048 B rows at
   a dense 2048 B stride, cross-wave: 484 of 868-942) next to cells it does

   before any MALL-blocking work in §5.1b/§2.4/§3.3, which needs a number to

8. **IDEAS §2.4 — workgroup swizzle.** Still cheap and structural, and the
   traversal axis sharpens what it would be testing: a swizzle changes
   exactly which addresses are in flight together, which is now a measured
   axis with a model behind it. But its bandwidth premise is gone — §2.3

3	// The dense bank at 4.5 bits: LLM.md L8c-4.
4	//
5	// L8a and L8b staged every dense weight in the width the checkpoint already
6	// ships — int8 with an fp16 scale per 32 — which is bit-identical arithmetic
7	// and took a decode token from 9.67 GB to 6.05. That is where the
8	// *checkpoint's* width runs out. L8c then measured what a narrower one costs,
9	// and the answer turned twice: symmetric Q4 at 4.5 bits is +18.5% of
10	// perplexity, and ggml's **asymmetric** K-quant at the same 4.500 bits is
11	// +7.04% uncalibrated and **+4.24% with unsloth's published imatrix**
12	// (L8c-3). So this is the bank that measurement recommends: 4.264 GB a token
13	// against 6.334 and a 56.7 tok/s ceiling against 38.2.
14	//
15	// # The layout
16	//
17	// Everything about it is §2.8's fragment tiling with a *nibble* where L8a
18	// puts a byte, plus a second plane that is ggml's own super-block record.
19	//
20	//	tiles    tile (nt, kt) is 128 contiguous bytes, kt fastest inside an
21	//	         n-tile, holding element (k, n) of the matrix at nibble
22	//	         (n%16)*16 + k%16 — byte (n%16)*8 + (k%16)/2, low nibble for
23	//	         even k. So a `uint` is eight consecutive k of one output
24	//	         column, where L8a's is four.
25	//
26	//	records  one per (n-tile, super-block, row): `d` and `dmin` as halves
27	//	         and then the 6-bit (scale, min) pair of every group, which is
28	//	         **sixteen bytes at eight groups** — ggml's own
29	//	         `get_scale_min_k4` record — and **twenty at ten** (see below).
30	//	         Indexed ((nt*nsb + sb)*16 + n%16), so the sixteen records a
31	//	         tile column needs are one contiguous run — the same k-major
32	//	         arrangement D8 chose for L8a's scale plane, for the same
33	//	         reason.
34	//
35	// 4 bits of level, 12 bits a group of 32 and 32 bits a super-block of 256 is
36	// **4.500 bits a weight**, which is the number every L8c-3 rung is quoted at.
37	//
38	// # The 320-wide family, and the one place this is not ggml
39	//
40	// A super-block is ggml's eight groups wherever `k % 256 == 0`, which is
41	// every dense matrix in this model but one family. `hc_{attn,ffn}_up` and
42	// `output_hc_up` read the low-rank space and are 320 wide, so their
43	// super-block is the **whole row** — ten groups — exactly as the simulation
44	// L8c-3 measured them with (`asymSubBlocks`). What does not carry over is the
45	// record: `get_scale_min_k4` is four low pairs and four high ones and it is
46	// not a length, so a ten-group record uses `packScaleMin12` instead and is
47	// twenty bytes rather than sixteen. The levels, the scales and the mins are
48	// the simulation's to the bit; only where the bits sit differs.
